name: BLIS (BLAS-like Library Instantiation Software)
baseline: OpenBLAS (the same graphs also compare Eigen, Intel MKL, ARMPL on Arm and Fujitsu SSL2 on A64fx)
workload: Level-3 BLAS (gemm, hemm/symm, herk/syrk, trmm, trsm) on square matrices (m=n=k) in single/double real and complex, single-threaded and multithreaded, reported in GFLOPS (per core when multithreaded) on ThunderX2, SkylakeX, Haswell, Zen, Zen2, A64fx and Neoverse N1; a second page covers small-matrix gemm.
claimed_speedup: The page gives graphs, not a numeric table. Its text says: 'OpenBLAS lags far behind MKL and BLIS due to lack of full support for AVX-512' (SkylakeX); 'MKL performance is dismal' (AMD Zen) and 'once again underwhelming' (AMD Zen2), the two platforms where BLIS is compared against it; 'MKL yields superb performance for most operations, though BLIS is not far behind except for trsm' (SkylakeX); 'pleasantly surprised by how competitive BLIS performs relative to MKL' (Haswell).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 6.3.0 (Haswell), gcc 7.3.0 (SkylakeX, Zen, ThunderX2), gcc 9.3.0 (Zen2), gcc 10.1.0 (A64fx), gcc 10.3.0 (Neoverse N1). BLIS built with './configure -t openmp auto' (sub-configurations such as skx and zen2); Eigen built with -march=native added to CXX_FLAGS; OpenBLAS built with Makefile.rule options listed on the page. Explicit BLIS CFLAGS are not listed (configure defaults).
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8167M (SkylakeX, 2 sockets x 26 cores), Intel Xeon E5-2690 v3 (Haswell), AMD Epyc 7551 (Zen1), AMD Epyc 7742 (Zen2), Marvell ThunderX2 CN9975, Fujitsu A64fx, AWS Graviton2 (Neoverse N1)
stars_or_usage: 2.7k stars; 2023 James H. Wilkinson Prize for Numerical Software (per the repo README page)
tradeoffs: ISO C99 framework with BLAS, CBLAS and its own typed/object APIs, so it links from C++ directly. Runtime sub-configuration selection ('auto'). It provides BLAS-like operations only, so full LAPACK needs libflame or another LAPACK on top. MKL stays faster on Intel hardware (SkylakeX) per the same page.
caveats: Results were gathered 2019-2021 against OpenBLAS 0.3.5/0.3.10/0.3.17 and MKL 2018-2020, so OpenBLAS (which later gained better AVX-512 kernels) and MKL have since changed. Run by the BLIS developers, though the benchmark driver code is public (test/3 in the repo). Win over MKL on AMD may reflect MKL's CPU dispatch rather than kernel quality (the authors speculate this on the page). Win over OpenBLAS is stated for SkylakeX only in text; other platforms need the graphs read. Explicit BLIS compiler flags are not listed, so tier A rests on the public driver, compiler version, CPU model and configure line.
found_via: PyPI simple-index scan for names matching blis/gemm/blas surfaced the 'blis' wheel (explosion/cython-blis, which bundles BLIS); then GitHub topic pages https://github.com/topics/blas?l=c and https://github.com/topics/dgemm list flame/blis; docs/Performance.md and docs/PerformanceSmall.md read from the repo. vcpkg and Conan Center have no BLIS port.

name: TBLIS (Tensor-Based Library Instantiation Software)
baseline: BLAS-based TTGT tensor contraction (transpose-transpose-GEMM-transpose around a BLAS GEMM such as OpenBLAS or MKL)
workload: Tensor contraction (a multi-dimensional generalisation of GEMM) done natively with BLIS-style micro-kernels, without the explicit tensor transpositions that a GEMM-based approach needs.
claimed_speedup: Wiki home page: TBLIS implements tensor contraction 'with essentially zero overhead compared to matrix multiplication'. The numeric comparison against TTGT is in the linked SISC paper (arXiv:1607.00291), which this agent could not open; no number is claimed here.
tradeoffs: C and C++ interfaces (tblis.h header in the repo); builds on BLIS-style kernels and its own threading; the wiki lists build/usage pages. Tensor operations only, not a drop-in BLAS replacement.
caveats: Evidence tier B rests on the peer-reviewed paper that the wiki's Research page cites (it says 'submitted to SISC'), but arxiv.org and the publisher were blocked in this container, so the speedup numbers, CPU, compiler and flags were not read. The repo README and wiki home contain no benchmark numbers. A verifier should open the paper and upgrade, downgrade or fill compiler/hardware.
found_via: Web search 'TBLIS tensor contraction library GitHub devinamatthews performance versus TTGT BLAS' after bassoy/ttv (already in this wave) benchmarked TBLIS 1.0.0 as a comparator; the PyPI scan also showed the pytblis and pyscf-tblis binding wheels. Pages opened: repo, wiki home, wiki Research page, commits page.

name: tblis-strassen (Strassen's Algorithm for Tensor Contraction)
baseline: TBLIS regular tensor-contraction routine (Strassen level L=0 in the same code); TBLIS is itself the state-of-the-art non-BLAS contraction library
workload: Synthetic tensor contractions and the Tensor Contraction Benchmark (TCCG 'tcb' set) on single-core, multicore and distributed-memory systems, using Strassen's algorithm inside a transposition-free contraction.
tradeoffs: Research code built on a copy of TBLIS and BLIS; test_strassen driver and tcb_run_*.sh scripts; build and run steps are described in artifact.pdf in the repo. Strassen adds extra additions and workspace use, and only pays off for large enough contractions.
caveats: The README cites a FLAME working note (TR-17-02) and an arXiv preprint (1704.03092); the TBLIS wiki says the paper was submitted to SC'18. Peer review was not confirmed from an opened page, so it stays at C; a verifier who confirms publication can raise it to B. Compiler, flags and CPU are in artifact.pdf, which this agent did not read. Repo has had no commits since 2017.
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/tensor-contraction (listing flame/tblis-strassen); README and commits page opened; the claim was cross-checked against the TBLIS wiki Research page.

name: Blaze
baseline: Eigen and Intel MKL (inferred: the README points to a Benchmarks wiki section that this agent could not open, so the exact comparison set is unconfirmed)
workload: Dense and sparse vector/matrix arithmetic with smart expression templates; dense matrix multiplication and other BLAS-level operations through manually tuned kernels or a linked BLAS.
claimed_speedup: README: 'one of the most intuitive and fastest C++ math libraries available'; 'impressive performance in the Benchmarks section'. No numbers on any page that was opened.
stars_or_usage: Ports in both vcpkg (3.8.2) and Conan Center; read-only GitHub mirror https://github.com/live-clones/blaze has 12 stars; latest release 3.8.2 (2020-08-15)
tradeoffs: Header-only; uses a BLAS (or its own kernels) for large dense products; SSE/AVX/AVX-512/FMA vectorisation; threading through OpenMP, HPX or C++11/Boost threads; padding is used for aligned SIMD access.
caveats: Tier D: the Blazemark benchmark wiki on bitbucket returned 404 to this agent, so no number could be checked. The only third-party result opened is the Fastor project's benchmark wiki (Blaze 3.7 vs Eigen 3.3.7, MKL JIT, LIBXSMM, Fastor on small fixed-size matrix products), which says Blaze with padding is 'in general being about 50% slower' than Fastor and 'over 2X slower in some cases', so the speed claim does not hold up in that small-matrix setting. Last commit date is from the GitHub mirror; the canonical bitbucket repo may be newer.
found_via: vcpkg versions/baseline.json scan (port 'blaze', description 'high-performance C++ math library') and Conan Center probe (recipes/blaze/config.yml exists); README read from the GitHub mirror; Fastor wiki Benchmarks page for the third-party comparison.

name: fmm-gen (Generating Families of Practical Fast Matrix Multiplication Algorithms)
baseline: conventional GEMM (the paper's classical dgemm; the opened pages do not name the library, so BLIS, MKL or OpenBLAS as comparator is unconfirmed)
workload: Generated Strassen-like fast matrix multiplication (20+ algorithm variants, multi-level, arbitrary matrix sizes and shapes) with the matrix additions fused into GEMM packing and micro-kernels, run on single-core and multicore systems and compared with a performance model.
claimed_speedup: README abstract: 'Our implementations demonstrate a performance benefit over conventional GEMM on single core and multi-core systems.' No numeric speedup appears on any opened page.
tradeoffs: Python scripts generate and compile C code per algorithm and partition (OpenMP, config.py and SLURM scripts for cluster runs). Fast matrix multiplication trades numerical stability and extra additions for fewer multiplications, and only helps above some matrix size; no BLAS-compatible drop-in interface is shown.
caveats: Tier B rests on the IPDPS 2017 paper (Huang, Rice, Matthews, van de Geijn) cited in the README's BibTeX; the paper PDF host was blocked in this container, so no speedup number, CPU, compiler or comparator library was read. The README says only that results should follow the paper's curves and that absolute GFLOPS differ by machine. Repo has had no commits since 2017. The related arbenson/fast-matmul project is already catalogued separately.
found_via: Related-links section of the flame/tblis-strassen README (opened), then the fmm-gen README, repo page, commits page and LICENSE (opened).
